business.title: Evaluating waste based retrofit strategies for thermal performance improvement in North Sinai social housing
business.desc: This study investigates thermal retrofitting strategies for single-family social housing in North Sinai, Egypt, with potential relevance to national decarbonization objectives. The research evaluates the thermal performance of locally sourced by-product materials, including barley straw (BS) and date palm (DP) waste, incorporated into compressed earth masonry and prefabricated cladding systems. These waste-based alternatives are benchmarked against the Egyptian residential building energy efficiency (RBEE) code and conventional synthetic insulation. Dynamic thermal simulations were conducted for the hot-humid climate of Bir El-Abd under both natural ventilation (NV) and mixed-mode ventilation (MMV) conditions. Simulation results indicate that the proposed interventions improved thermal performance relative to the baseline model. Under NV, the 15 cm BS masonry reduced annual discomfort hours by 23.7%, achieving approximately 89% of the discomfort reduction observed in the 60 cm theoretical variant. Under MMV, this configuration reduced annual cooling electricity use by 27.9%, with operational CO2 emissions decreasing to approximately 939.3 kg. Compared with the 15 cm BS masonry, the 6 cm DPM panel achieved a 21.9% reduction in discomfort hours and a 28.8% reduction in annual total heating and cooling electricity use for the South orientation. While BS masonry demonstrated higher thermal performance, the DPM cladding may offer a lower-profile alternative with reduced spatial impact. These results suggest that localized biocomposites may offer a potential pathway for reducing energy use and operational emissions in similar residential retrofit contexts.

business.title: Adaptive generalized regressive deep convolutional reinforcement learning for crop yield prediction in smart precision farming
business.desc: Accurate crop yield assessment is essential for improving agricultural productivity and resource management. However, yield prediction is challenging due to multiple influencing factors such as soil properties, weather conditions, crop practices, pests, and diseases. While deep learning techniques have improved prediction capabilities, achieving high accuracy with low error and reduced computation time remains a key concern for large-scale datasets. To address this, an Adaptive Generalized Regressive Deep Convolutional Reinforcement Learning (AGR-DCRL) model is proposed to enhance prediction accuracy for smart farming. The model consists of input, convolution, pooling and dense layers. Data is first collected in data harvesting using IoT technologies that monitor weather, soil conditions, and pesticide usage. During data augmentation, Adaptive proximity sampling process is utilized in input layer to create new data samples. In the convolution layer, preprocessing is performed by using weighted local similarity-based imputation and Generalized Tietjen–Moore test. The missing values are handled and outlier’s are detected. Feature selection is applied in pooling layer using Camargo’s adaptive diversity index to select the most relevant features and remove irrelevant features for reducing the dimensionality. Crop yield prediction is performed at dense layer for analyzing both extracted features and data samples via polytomous logistic regression. The output layer employs a softmax activation function to create multi-class prediction results. Then, the error rate is measured with each prediction outcome and rewards. The Q-values are iteratively updated based on rewards until the model converges. Lastly, the accurate crop yield prediction is obtained with higher accuracy and lesser error. Experimental assessment of the proposed technique is implanted in Python using Smart Farming Sensor Data for Yield Prediction dataset with several metrics. Experimental results demonstrate that the AGR-DCRL model achieves higher accuracy by 4%, lesser error rates by 69%, and faster prediction time by 20% compared to conventional deep learning approaches.

business.title: Safety, tolerability, and gastrointestinal effect of a Bifidobacterium-based synergistic synbiotic in infants and toddlers
business.desc: Bifidobacterium are critical components of the infant gut microbiome, yet most infants in developed countries are deficient. The ARTEMIS trial is the first clinical study in the United States to evaluate a synergistic synbiotic supplement in infants. It enrolled 114 participants in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study conducted to evaluate the safety, tolerability, and gastrointestinal colonization of the supplement in infants (n = 58) and toddlers (n = 56). The synbiotic contains four proprietary strains of Bifidobacterium, four complementary human milk oligosaccharides and vitamin D. Safety and tolerability were assessed, with no statistically significant differences in adverse events or gastrointestinal symptom burden relative to placebo. The administered Bifidobacterium strains were significantly more prevalent and abundant in the synbiotic group. After four weeks of dosing, at least one administered strain was detected in 72% of infants (2–12 months) and 67% of toddlers (12–24 months). Synbiotic supplementation was associated with a significant increase in Bifidobacterium infantis abundance at the species level and human milk oligosaccharide utilization genes. Strains persisted through the two-week washout period, supporting intestinal colonization beyond active supplementation unlike other transient probiotics like Lactobacillus. This synbiotic was safe, well tolerated, and achieved sustained Bifidobacterium colonization in infants and toddlers.

business.title: Morphology-aware supervision improves real-time wind turbine blade defect localization in unstructured natural environments
business.desc: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) inspection is widely used for wind turbine blade maintenance, yet detecting minor damage in operational wind farms remains difficult because background clutter, extreme defect aspect ratios, and curved or bifurcated image-space geometries all reduce accuracy. We propose SWCB-YOLO, a lightweight edge detector built on YOLOv11n. Its central contribution is a Curvature-Aware Shape IoU (CA-Shape-IoU) loss, a morphology-aware image-space localization regularizer whose supervision derives from crack morphology: Bézier-curvature, skeleton-distance, and elongation fields are precomputed offline from polygon masks and applied during training, leaving the detection head and inference cost unchanged. The loss is paired with an Asymmetric Strip Swin-TransformerV2 (AS-Swin2) module for long-range dependencies along slender cracks and a Frequency-Spatial Dual-Domain Attention (FS-DDA) module that combines DCT-informed channel recalibration with spatial attention. On a field dataset spanning a full annual cycle, SWCB-YOLO attains 89.0% mAP@50 and 52.8% mAP@50:95, improving on the YOLOv11n baseline by 13.8 and 11.7 percentage points under a common training protocol, with 3.70M parameters at 35 FPS on a Jetson Xavier NX. The improvement remains positive in every turbine-grouped cross-validation fold (+12.4 to +14.6 points) and after near-duplicate test frames are removed. Evaluation on five open benchmarks, including two blade-defect datasets, further examines transfer beyond the development site; the implementation and benchmark configurations are publicly available.

technology.title: BOE hopes to be Apple's second supplier for the 2027 OLED iPad Air and future MacBook laptops
technology.desc: For its 2026 new device lineup, Apple has decided to rely exclusively on OLED panels produced by Samsung Display and LG Display. This has been a setback for BOE , that hoped to enter the supply chain. But it seems as if Apple did not want to take this change, following BEO's consistent quality and production issues.But BOE is not giving up, and a new report from Korea suggests that BOE is developing OLED tablet panels, hoping to enter Apple's supply chain for the 2027 iPad Air, that will utilize an AMOLED display. Apple has already selected Samsung Display as its main supplier for these OLED iPad Air panels, but BOE wishes to become Apple's second supplier. BOE develops these new panels at its B12 6-Gen OLED production line in Chongqing. Apple iPad Air OLED will have 11" and 13" displays, both based on TFE-on-glass (hybrid OLED), LTPS backplanes, single-stack OLED architecture and a 60 Hz refresh rate.The panels are at an early stage of development, but BOE is expected to be able to ship samples for Apple soon. Apple will likely make the decision regarding BOE's panels towards the end of 2026. If BOE does not make the cut, Samsung Display will remain an exclusive supplier - this won't be a surprise - in 2026 Apple has selected SDC as its exclusive supplier for its Foldable iPhone, it's iPad Mini and the 14-inch and 16-inch Macbook Pro laptops.In addition to the tablet displays, BOE is also hoping to enter Apple's laptop supply chain, perhaps as soon as in 2028 for the MacBOok Pro OLEDs. technology.title: Xiaomi launches new smartphones that feature the company's self-developed green pTSF OLED emitters
technology.desc: Xiaomi launched two smartphones yesterday, the Redmi K100 Pro and the Redmi K100 Pro Max. The K100 Pro features a 6.59" 185Hz 4,500 nits (peak) 1156x2510 full-RGB AMOLED display, while the K100 Pro Max increases the display size to 6.9", with a 1200x2608 resolution.Xiaomi says that this is the first smartphone to utilize its new self-developed green pTSF emitter system. The company says it developed this new emitter system in collaboration with researchers at Tsinghua University. It is likely that the actual panel producer is Visionox - that also has strong ties to Tsinghua University (as it was founded as a University spinoff back in 2001), and Visionox indeed started producing commercial OLED displays with green pTSF OLED emitter systems earlier this year. Last year Xioami developed its own red OLED emitter system, probably based on phosphorescence emitters. It is not clear whether these new smartphones utilize also the company's red emitters. Interestingly, there was an online mention that Xiaomi is referring to the OLED stack as the "M11 OLED", which is similar to Samsung Display's naming schemes. You can learn more about Visionox's pTSF / PSF OLED emitter systems here and in our latest Visionox Spotlight article.
